results.title: Natural beauty made this New Zealand tourist village. Now it threatens its existence
results.description: Famed for its nearby glacier, Franz Josef village faces ‘catastrophic’ flooding and deaths if action not taken to manage the Waiho River The small village of Franz Josef sits on the rugged west coast of New Zealand’s South Island, its natural beauty providing the drawcard for a million tourists to pack its hotels, spas and restaurants every year. But that drawcard – which has turned it into a hotspot for everything from hiking to kayaking and made it one of the country’s most popular destinations – may change the course of the village’s fate once again. results.title: My prognosis for 2027
results.description: IN A word, it’s grim, reflecting a dangerous convergence of acute natural hazards and escalating human-induced threats. We must build our resilience in preparation for the compound shocks that could impact us, more importantly, our citizens most at risk, and still emerge intact. I. Natural and ecological threats to national security Natural hazards in the Philippines are no longer isolated seasonal disruptions; they have become persistent national security multipliers that directly degrade food, water and energy stability: – The Manila Trench megathrust and tsunami hazard: Scientific modeling and DOST-Phivolcs assessments highlight the catastrophic potential of the Manila Trench, an active subduction zone stretching from the Ilocos region to Mindoro. Capable of generating a megaquake of up to magnitude 8.4, a rupture could trigger tsunami waves reaching 5.5 meters or higher, extending up to 2.7 kilometers inland across 66 coastal areas, including Western Luzon, Mimaropa, and low-lying Metro Manila corridors via Manila Bay and the Pasig River, crippling major port and energy terminals, and severing supply lines. – Intensifying “very strong” El Niño and drought: DOST-Pag-Asa has warned of a “very strong” El Niño persisting through the first half of 2027, projected to bring drought conditions across nearly all provinces by March 2027. Depleted watersheds cripple agricultural yields, dry up water reservoirs, and slash hydroelectric power generation just as extreme heat surges, spikes cooling demand, and destabilizes the power grid. – Super typhoons, flooding and inland seismic threats: Increasingly destructive typhoons repeatedly wipe out rural livelihoods and disrupt logistics flows, alongside geophysical risks from the West Valley Fault and active volcanoes such as Taal, Mayon and Kanlaon, capable of paralyzing our nerve centers overnight. – Transboundary health and biosecurity risks: High population density and fragmented health care capacity leave communities acutely exposed to vectorborne outbreaks, agricultural pests, and emerging infectious diseases that thrive during extreme climate swings. 2. Human-induced and geopolitical threats Layered atop these ecological insecurities is an array of human-induced threats: – Compounding global wars (Ukraine and Iran/Middle East): We face a dual-front external supply shock. The prolonged war in Ukraine continues to distort global food and fertilizer markets, driving up agricultural input costs, and inflating staple food prices while dislocating global supply chains. On top of this, the 2026 war on Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz directly threaten our imports of around 98 percent of our crude oil requirements. A protracted Middle East conflict risks recurring fuel shortages, power grid red alerts, airline and transport disruptions, and peril to millions of OFWs whose remittances keep domestic consumption afloat. – Maritime coercion and regional flashpoints: China’s escalating grayzone aggression in the West Philippine Sea (deliberate ramming, obstructing resupply missions and naval intimidation) endangers our territorial integrity and maritime sovereign rights, fisherfolk and offshore energy exploration. Beyond the EEZ, the proliferation of drugs and sleeper cells; fake citizens acquiring property, mining our mineral resources, and embedding themselves in society; illegal businesses that produce substandard steel, scams and serve as hubs for money laundering and gambling; and subversion in low and high places are major national security risks. A potential conflict across the First Island Chain (including a Taiwan contingency) risks severing vital sea lines of communication (SLOCs) and drawing us to rescue trapped OFWs through hostile airspace and troubled waters. – Macroeconomic fragility and imported inflation: Sluggish growth, a weakened peso, and stagflation create a regressive squeeze on low-income households. Because food, transport, water and electricity consume most of the poor’s budgets, more price shocks threaten to push millions more into poverty and ignite social riots. Escalating AI-driven disinformation, deepfakes, cyber intrusions and cyberattacks globally, targeting government agencies, financial networks, health care systems and critical industrial control (Scada) infrastructure, are causing widespread alarm. – Political polarization, the Sara Duterte impeachment fallout, and governance failure: As the Senate impeachment trial of Sara Duterte approaches its conclusion, a conviction risks polarization, leading to mass protests and destabilization attempts. Conversely, budget discrepancies, flood-control graft, and persistent governance failure erode institutional legitimacy and public trust. When citizens view state institutions as selfserving or paralyzed by elite power struggles, rather than focused on survival and basic services, mobilizing society for whole-of-nation activism will be extremely difficult. 3. Why economic and political fragility is a national security crisis In reality, policymaking, economic welfare, political stability, disaster response, and military defense form a single human and national security continuum. An economy where millions live on the edge, governed by institutions fractured by partisan warfare, is strategically brittle. When the civilian home front is hungry, angry, divided and financially exhausted, military deterrence will not hold. Adversaries employing hybrid warfare won’t need to launch a massive conventional attack to bring a vulnerable nation to its knees. A maritime blockade, cyber-induced blackouts, targeted kinetic attacks on centers of gravity, disinformation campaigns, and sponsored violence can induce strategic paralysis from within. 4. The imperative: Integrating civil and national defense Surviving future shocks requires abandoning our reactive, post-disaster relief mindset in favor of preparedness as the new paradigm cutting across communities, businesses, LGUs, and security institutions First, civil defense must be decentralized to our barangay (villages). True civil resilience means building self-reliant neighborhoods capable of looking after their welfare for an indefinite period while frontliners are sidelined, to enable the State to reconstitute itself and focus on its missions. Second, critical infrastructure and business continuity must be hardened to avoid becoming single points of failure. This demands strict physical and cyber isolation of industrial control systems, expanded strategic reserves, and mandatory business continuity planning to protect the balance sheet, stakeholders, and to keep the goods and services flowing. Third, while the AFP sustains its modernization and professionalization campaigns to achieve credible deterrence, a redeveloped and restructured Reserve Force will serve as an interoperable civil-military bridge, capable of executing hybrid missions in support. Finally, good governance must serve as the bedrock of resilience to sustain the nation despite potentially crippling sudden impacts in the coming year. Leadership for building resilience and shared prosperity, despite troubling times, is what 2027 will demand from all of us. Rafael M. Alunan III, the incoming president of the Management Association of the Philippines, is a former interior and local government secretary.
creator: rafael alunan iii
